name: Pale Chalcedony Yellow
lede: Pale Chalcedony Yellow is a soft, pale cream-yellow, built by putting the modifier pale in front of the base color [[chalcedony-yellow]], named for the pale yellow banding seen in the mineral chalcedony.

sections.title: A modifier on a mineral's name
sections.body:
Pale Chalcedony Yellow puts the modifier word pale in front of the base color [[chalcedony-yellow]], in the compound-modifier grammar our library uses for names like this one [1]. The base name points to chalcedony, a waxy quartz that can show pale, honeyed bands, though our data does not go further into which specific stone or supplier set the standard swatch [1]. Robert Ridgway first listed it in his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, plate XVII, hue 25, tone f, and the Inter-Society Color Council later filed it in the ISCC-NBS 1955 system as block 104 (R) [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[pale-goldenrod]], only 2.5 units off, close enough on screen to read as the same pale yellow [2]; [[lemon-meringue]] and [[seafoam]] both sit 3.0 units away [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color within range of this swatch in 487 of 23,781 paintings, 2.05 percent, as photographed; looking for real coverage inside each painting narrows that to 270 [3]. That makes it more common than 75 percent of the named colors in our library [3]. It most often plays a light, in 73 percent of its 270 appearances by lightness rank, so varnish cannot fake the result [3]. John Singer Sargent is its most devoted painter, present in 12 of his 287 works here, 2.9 times the expected rate for the museums those paintings come from [3].

The earliest match dates to 1413, exactly five hundred years before Ridgway's 1912 plate, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin; it marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment or mineral [3].
